content.title: About
content.content: Beef cooked in a soy‑based sauce consists of tender pieces of meat marinated and simmered in soy sauce with spices. The dish combines a rich meaty flavor with a subtle sweet‑salty note typical of Asian cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soy sauce has been used in cooking for over 2,500 years, originating in China.
Traditionally, beef in soy sauce is slow‑cooked to become melt‑in‑the‑mouth and fully infused with flavor.
The beef‑soy combination is popular in dishes such as beef stroganoff and Chinese‑style beef stir‑fry.
Fermentation of soy sauce creates amino acids that enhance umami taste.
Japan’s “tamari” soy sauce is less salty and often preferred for marinating meat.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef supplies easily absorbable heme iron, important for blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: With soy sauce as the main source of carbs, the meal fits low‑carb diets.

items.title: Antioxidants from soy sauce
items.content: Fermented soy sauce contains polyphenols that may have antioxidant effects.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce is salty; people with hypertension should limit portion size.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy products.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Beef contains saturated fat, so choosing lean cuts is advisable.

items.title: Meat quality control
items.content: Use fresh beef to avoid the risk of foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course with rice, noodles, or vegetable sides. Leftovers reheat well in a microwave or skillet, adding a splash of water to keep the meat moist.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked beef in soy sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in freezer‑safe bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

corn-canned-cooked-with-butter-or-margar.title: Corn, canned, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Corn, canned, cooked with butter or margarine (code 4680) is a ready‑to‑eat product made from mature sweet corn kernels that are boiled, mixed with butter or margarine, and sealed in airtight cans. The product retains a sweet flavor, tender texture, and a buttery aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned corn is a staple side dish in American and European cuisines because it requires no preparation.
Adding butter or margarine improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin A and K.
Corn is one of the few vegetables that naturally contains appreciable amounts of carotenoids, giving it a golden hue.
In the United States, over 70 % of all canned vegetables are corn varieties.
Corn was one of the first domesticated crops, cultivated by humans more than 7,000 years ago.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Corn provides fiber that supports healthy digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product contains thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Carotenoids
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin help maintain eye health and protect against age‑related macular degeneration.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Corn supplies magnesium, potassium, and iron, essential for muscle function and blood formation.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Its carbohydrate content provides a quick source of energy, while the added fats make the dish more satiating.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Although uncommon, corn allergy can cause skin rashes, swelling, and respiratory symptoms.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet corn naturally contains sugars; individuals with diabetes should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Trans fats in margarine
items.content: If prepared with margarine, the product may contain trans fats, which should be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, soups, pasta, omelets, or used as a filling for tacos and burritos. Warm it briefly in a skillet with a little butter for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer the corn to an airtight container and keep it refrigerated for up to 3–4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit juice drink, light is a non‑alcoholic beverage made from filtered fruit juices with minimal sugar and low calorie content. It combines apple, pear and berry juices, natural flavorings and added B‑vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink contains no added sugar; the sweetener used is stevia.
It is fortified with vitamin C to support the immune system.
The light version provides about 30 kcal per 100 ml, making it popular among weight‑conscious consumers.
Natural flavor extracts preserve the bright taste of fresh fruit.
Packaged in recyclable aluminum cans to reduce environmental impact.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Approximately 30 kcal per 100 ml helps maintain a balanced energy intake.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: Made mostly of water, it contributes to the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: No artificial colourings
items.content: Only natural extracts are used, reducing the risk of allergic reactions.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B2 and B6 aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Allergy to fruit components
items.content: Individuals allergic to apples, pears or berries may experience reactions.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The drink’s acidity may irritate a sensitive stomach when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Not suitable for infants under 1 year
items.content: Due to potential allergenicity and acidity, it is not recommended for babies.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: High doses of vitamin C can affect the efficacy of certain drugs, such as anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Consume chilled as a refreshing snack, after workouts, or as an alternative to sugary sodas. It can also be added to smoothies to boost fruit flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Garlic Bread with Parmesan is a crunchy slice of bread brushed with fragrant garlic butter and sprinkled with grated Parmesan cheese, then baked to a golden crust. It is commonly served in fast‑food outlets and restaurants as an appetizer or side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first garlic bread recipe appeared in Italy in the early 20th century.
Parmesan (Parmigiano‑Reggiano) is protected by a geographical indication and is produced only in specific Italian provinces.
Garlic bread is often served with marinara or cheese sauce.
The combination of garlic and Parmesan enhances aromatic compounds, creating a richer flavor.
In the United States, garlic bread with Parmesan became popular in the 1990s thanks to chain pizzerias.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Garlic contains allicin, an antioxidant that supports the immune system.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Garlic sulfides may help lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Hard Parmesan provides significant amounts of calcium and phosphorus, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Parmesan adds both dairy and plant‑based protein, contributing to satiety.

items.title: Probiotic effect
items.content: Fermented cheese contains probiotic cultures that support gut microbiota.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Parmesan can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Hard cheese is salty, so individuals with hypertension should limit portion size.

items.title: Gas and discomfort
items.content: Garlic may cause bloating and heartburn in some individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively high in calories due to butter and cheese; moderate portions are recommended.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Garlic can enhance the effect of anticoagulants, so caution is advised for those on blood thinners.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, straight from the oven. Cut into bite‑size pieces and enjoy as a snack, add to salads or soups, or use as a base for sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze for up to 1 month.

seafood-garden-salad-with-seafood-lettuc.title: Seafood garden salad with seafood, lettuce, eggs, tomato and/or carrots, other vegetables, no dressing

content.title: About
content.content: The Seafood garden salad combines fresh seafood (shrimp, mussels, squid), crisp lettuce, boiled eggs, tomatoes, carrots and other vegetables. It is served without any dressing, allowing the natural flavors of the ingredients to shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The salad blends a marine theme with garden freshness, highlighting a wide range of tastes and textures.
Seafood is usually steamed or quickly sautéed to retain tenderness and nutrients.
Eggs add protein and a bright color, making the dish more visually appealing.
Tomatoes and carrots are rich in antioxidants such as lycopene and beta‑carotene.
The lack of dressing makes the salad suitable for those watching calories and fat intake.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Seafood and eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Shrimp and fish contain EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and seafood are rich in B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes, carrots and lettuce supply lycopene, beta‑carotene and vitamin C, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low added fat
items.content: Serving the salad without dressing reduces added fats and calories, making it a light option.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels or squid.

items.title: Food poisoning risk
items.content: Seafood must be fresh and properly handled; otherwise bacterial contamination is possible.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor egg intake.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Non‑organic vegetables may carry pesticide residues; thorough washing is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad cold, immediately after preparation. It can be enjoyed as a standalone meal or as a side dish. If desired, a squeeze of lemon juice or fresh herbs can be added for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Longer storage may cause seafood to lose freshness and become a bacterial hazard.
